exonerate

/ig-ZON-uh-rayt/ - the stress falls on ZON · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Exonerate means to officially clear someone of guilt or blame.

The observatory's own photographic plates exonerated the night assistant, fixing the comet fraud on a visiting scholar instead.

Example

The stagecoach driver lost his post over the missing mailbag and spent two years hauling stone; when the sorting-room floorboards finally came up and the bag was found where a clerk had hidden it, the service exonerated him publicly and restored his route.

Exonerate is the most official of the clearing words — it comes from boards, courts, and reviews, and it often arrives after punishment has already fallen, wiping the record clean. The Latin means 'to unload a burden,' and that is its exact feel: the accusation's weight lifted off.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

reinstate: To reinstate someone is to return them to the post or rank an accusation cost them — a practical restoration of the job itself. Exonerate works on the record instead: a board officially clears the accusation and wipes the stain away. A service may exonerate a driver yet fail to reinstate him.

rehabilitate: To rehabilitate someone is to restore their reputation and standing gradually, often years after the harm was done. Exonerate is the sharper official act: a board or review formally declares the person clear of the charge in one stroke. Rehabilitation mends opinion; exoneration fixes the record.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

convict: to find guilty — the opposite ruling

accuse: to lay the charge in the first place

Where it sits · how fully innocence is established

excuse → acquit → exonerate

excuse vs. exonerate: To excuse a small lapse is to wave it off in the moment; excuse stops far short of exonerate, which formally erases a grave accusation.

acquit vs. exonerate: A jury acquits when guilt is not proven; acquit stops short of exonerate, which declares the accused actually innocent and scrubs the record clean.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-: off, away

Root — oner: burden, load

Suffix — -ate: to make, to do

Put it together: Ex- (off) + oner (burden) + -ate (to make) = to take the burden off. Latin onus, oneris — 'a load' — still works in English: the onus of proof is the load an accuser must carry. To exonerate someone is to unload the accusation from their back.

Use the root in a new word: onus: The coach shrugged and said the onus was on the visiting team now.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / official

Exonerate is the press-conference word: review boards and commissions exonerate, often years late. Beside its cousins here — exculpate (proof lifts blame), absolve (an authority lifts guilt or duty), vindicate (events prove you right) — exonerate stresses the official record set right.
